questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best explains the sentence: Though Mr. Iro is a new chairman, he views other members with a jaundiced eye.

options.text: He takes a rather forceful position on dealing with his members.
options.why: "Jaundiced" is about suspicion, not force.
options.whyWrong: "With a jaundiced eye" is about attitude, not force. It means he looks at them with suspicion or dislike.

options.text: He takes an unfavourable position concerning his members.
options.why: To view with a jaundiced eye means to regard with suspicion or disapproval.

options.text: He takes a sickly view of his members.
options.why: This takes "jaundiced" literally, as the illness.
options.whyWrong: Jaundice is an illness, but the idiom is figurative. It means an unfavourable, suspicious view, not a "sickly" one.

options.text: He takes a rather hazy view of his members.
options.why: "Hazy" means unclear, which is not the meaning.
options.whyWrong: A jaundiced eye is not unclear vision. It is a negative, distrustful attitude.

questions.explanation: "To view something with a jaundiced eye" means to regard it with suspicion, bitterness or disapproval. So the new chairman has an unfavourable attitude towards the other members.
questions.trap: C catches students who take "jaundiced" literally as the yellow-eye illness. Idioms are never read word for word.

askPresets.answer: If a new teacher sees the whole class as troublemakers before knowing them, she views them with a jaundiced eye.
Jaundice is an illness, but the idiom is figurative. It means an unfavourable, suspicious view, not a "sickly" one.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best explains the sentence: It is good to steer a middle course in whatever one does.

options.text: It is always good to get midway in anything one does.
options.why: This reads "middle" literally as halfway.
options.whyWrong: "Middle course" is not about stopping halfway. It means avoiding extremes, acting with moderation.

options.text: It is always good to act with moderation.
options.why: Steering a middle course means avoiding extremes, which is moderation.

options.text: It is always good to move away from the forefront.
options.why: This is about position, not behaviour.
options.whyWrong: The idiom says nothing about leaving the front. It is about balance between extremes.

options.text: It is always good to work very hard.
options.why: Working very hard is a different idea.
options.whyWrong: Hard work is good advice but not what the idiom says. A middle course means moderation.

questions.explanation: To steer a middle course means to take a balanced position between two extremes, that is, to act with moderation.
questions.trap: A catches students who take "middle" literally, as getting halfway through a task.
questions.mnemonic: Middle course = not too much, not too little.

askPresets.answer: Eating neither too much nor too little before an exam is steering a middle course.
"Middle course" is not about stopping halfway. It means avoiding extremes, acting with moderation.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best explains the sentence: The footballers moved with their tails between their legs.

options.text: They moved happily because they won the match.
options.why: This is the opposite feeling.
options.whyWrong: A tail between the legs is a sign of shame or defeat, not happiness.

options.text: They were unhappy because they had been despised by their opponents.
options.why: The idiom is about defeat and shame, not being despised.
options.whyWrong: Being despised is not the point. The idiom shows shame after losing.

options.text: They were ashamed because they had been defeated.
options.why: A dog puts its tail between its legs when beaten or scared, so the idiom means ashamed after defeat.

options.text: They moved with their tails between their legs.
options.why: This just repeats the idiom literally.
options.whyWrong: Footballers have no tails. Repeating the words does not explain the meaning: they were ashamed after being defeated.

questions.explanation: "With one's tail between one's legs" comes from a beaten dog. It describes someone leaving ashamed or humiliated after a defeat.
questions.trap: D simply repeats the idiom word for word. JAMB often includes this kind of option; it never explains the meaning.

askPresets.answer: Picture a dog that has just been scolded, slinking away with its tail tucked under.
Being despised is not the point. The idiom shows shame after losing.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best explains the sentence: As regards the matter, we have crossed the Rubicon.

options.text: We are completely at a loss.
options.why: Being at a loss means confused, which is not the meaning.
options.whyWrong: Crossing the Rubicon is about a firm decision, not confusion.

options.why: Crossing the Rubicon means taking a step that cannot be undone, so we are irrevocably committed.
Being qualified is unrelated.
options.whyWrong: The idiom has nothing to do with qualifications. It means there is no turning back.

options.why: Close, but "perfectly" misses the key idea of no return.
options.whyWrong: "Perfectly committed" sounds close, but the idiom stresses that the decision cannot be reversed: irrevocably.

questions.explanation: When Julius Caesar crossed the river Rubicon with his army, he started a war that could not be undone. To cross the Rubicon means to pass a point of no return, so to be irrevocably committed.
questions.trap: D looks almost the same as B. The difference is "irrevocably", meaning it cannot be reversed, which is the heart of the idiom.

askPresets.answer: Once you submit your JAMB form and pay, you have crossed the Rubicon on your subject choice.
"Perfectly committed" sounds close, but the idiom stresses that the decision cannot be reversed: irrevocably.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best explains the sentence: Uche is full of himself.

options.why: "Full of himself" means he thinks too highly of himself, which is conceited.
This reads "full" literally.
options.whyWrong: "Full of himself" is not about being complete. It means proud or self-important.

options.why: Wealth is not mentioned.
options.whyWrong: The idiom says nothing about money. It is about too much pride.

options.why: Carefulness is unrelated.
options.whyWrong: Being careful is a different quality. "Full of himself" means conceited.

questions.explanation: To be full of oneself means to be very proud of oneself and to think one is more important than others, that is, conceited.
questions.trap: B catches students who read "full" literally as complete.
questions.mnemonic: Full of himself = no space for others.

askPresets.answer: The classmate who only talks about his own scores is full of himself.
"Full of himself" is not about being complete. It means proud or self-important.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in quotes: I am optimistic about the interview though it was a "mindbending" exercise.

options.why: Enervating means tiring, which is similar, not opposite.
options.whyWrong: Enervating (tiring) is close in meaning to mindbending, not opposite.

options.why: Debilitating means weakening, similar not opposite.
options.whyWrong: Debilitating is close to mindbending (hard, draining). We need the opposite.

options.why: Difficult is a synonym.
options.whyWrong: Difficult means almost the same as mindbending. The opposite is easy.

options.why: Mindbending means very hard; the opposite is easy.

questions.explanation: Mindbending describes something so hard it strains the mind. Its opposite is easy.
questions.trap: Options A, B and C are all similar in meaning. In antonym questions, cross out every option that means the same.

askPresets.answer: If a puzzle is mindbending, the opposite puzzle is easy.
Difficult means almost the same as mindbending. The opposite is easy.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in quotes: The teacher said that Ali's essay was full of many "redundant" details.

options.why: Unexplained is not the opposite of unnecessary.
options.whyWrong: Redundant means not needed. Unexplained is a different idea.

options.why: Strange is unrelated.
options.whyWrong: Strange does not contrast with redundant.

options.why: Redundant means not needed; necessary is its opposite.
Close, but necessary is the direct opposite.
options.whyWrong: Useful is a reasonable contrast, but redundant means unnecessary, so the exact opposite is necessary.

questions.explanation: Redundant means more than needed, unnecessary. The opposite is necessary.
questions.trap: D, useful, is a near-opposite. JAMB wants the most exact opposite: necessary.

askPresets.answer: A tenth spare pen in your bag is redundant; your one working pen is necessary.
Useful is a reasonable contrast, but redundant means unnecessary, so the exact opposite is necessary.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in quotes: The captain says sports is being "debased" by commercial sponsorship.

options.why: Localized is unrelated.
options.whyWrong: Localized means limited to an area. It does not contrast with debased.

options.why: Perverted is a synonym.
options.whyWrong: Perverted (corrupted) is close to debased. We need the opposite.

options.why: Debased means lowered in value; elevated means raised.
Overvalued is about price, not quality.
options.whyWrong: Overvalued means priced too high. The opposite of debased (lowered in quality) is elevated.

questions.explanation: To debase is to lower the quality, value or dignity of something. The opposite is to elevate, to raise up.
questions.trap: B, perverted, means almost the same as debased. Spot synonyms and remove them.
questions.mnemonic: Debase = take down; elevate = lift up.

askPresets.answer: A base is at the bottom; to de-base is to bring down, to elevate is to lift up.
Perverted (corrupted) is close to debased. We need the opposite.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in quotes: There was a general "acquiescence" on the new drug law.

options.why: Acquiescence means quiet acceptance; resistance is the opposite.
Discrepancy means a difference, unrelated.
options.whyWrong: A discrepancy is a mismatch. It is not the opposite of acceptance.

options.why: Compromise is a middle ground.
options.whyWrong: Compromise is meeting halfway. The opposite of accepting is resisting.

options.why: Agreement is a synonym.
options.whyWrong: Agreement is close to acquiescence. We need the opposite: resistance.

questions.explanation: Acquiescence means accepting something quietly without protest. The opposite is resistance.
questions.trap: D, agreement, is a synonym. In antonym questions the synonym is the most common trap.
questions.mnemonic: Acquiesce = quietly say yes; resist = say no.

askPresets.answer: When everyone accepted the new school rule without complaint, that was acquiescence.
Agreement is close to acquiescence. We need the opposite: resistance.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option opposite in meaning to the word in quotes: The report of the committee contained a "plethora" of details.

options.why: Plethora means too many; shortage means too few.
Simplicity is about how easy, not how many.
options.whyWrong: Simplicity is not about number. The opposite of a great excess is a shortage.

options.why: Multitude is a synonym.
options.whyWrong: A multitude means a great number, close to plethora.

options.why: Spectrum means a range, unrelated.
options.whyWrong: A spectrum is a range. The opposite of plethora is shortage.

questions.explanation: A plethora is an excessive amount, far too much. The opposite is a shortage.
questions.trap: C, multitude, means a large number, so it is similar, not opposite.

askPresets.answer: A plethora of mangoes in season; a shortage of mangoes out of season.
A multitude means a great number, close to plethora.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in quotes: A political "impasse" does not offer the best opportunity for merrymaking.

options.why: A manifesto is a party's programme.
options.whyWrong: A manifesto is a statement of policies, not a deadlock.

options.why: A party is unrelated.
options.whyWrong: A party is a group or celebration. Impasse means deadlock.

options.why: An impasse is a deadlock where no progress is possible, like a gridlock.
A rally is a political gathering.
options.whyWrong: A rally fits the political setting but not the meaning. Impasse means deadlock.

questions.explanation: An impasse is a situation where no progress can be made because people cannot agree. Gridlock means the same.
questions.trap: D, rally, fits the political theme of the sentence, but the question is about the word's meaning, not the topic.

askPresets.answer: When traffic cannot move in any direction at a junction, that is gridlock, an impasse.
A rally fits the political setting but not the meaning. Impasse means deadlock.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in quotes: The law is often "tardy" in reacting to changing attitudes.

options.why: Quick is the opposite.
options.whyWrong: Quick is an antonym. Tardy means slow or late.

options.why: Tardy means slow or late.
Exclusive is unrelated.
options.whyWrong: Exclusive means limited to some people, unrelated to tardy.

options.why: Generous is unrelated.
options.whyWrong: Generous means giving freely, unrelated to tardy.

questions.explanation: Tardy means slow to act or late. The law is slow to react to changes in attitudes.
questions.trap: A, quick, is the opposite. Check whether the question asks for nearest or opposite meaning.

askPresets.answer: A student who comes in after assembly is tardy.
Quick is an antonym. Tardy means slow or late.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in quotes: The "panacea" for a country's economic mess lies in systematic planning and hard work.

options.why: A panacea is a cure or remedy for all problems.
Hope is a feeling, not a remedy.
options.whyWrong: Hope is related but not the meaning. A panacea is a cure.

options.why: Foresight is planning ahead.
options.whyWrong: Foresight is a quality, not a remedy. Panacea means cure.

options.why: Trouble is the opposite idea.
options.whyWrong: Trouble is the problem, not the remedy.

questions.explanation: A panacea is a remedy that solves all problems or cures all diseases. Here, the cure for the economy's problems.
questions.trap: B, hope, sounds positive and fits the sentence, but a panacea is a remedy, not a feeling.

askPresets.answer: Some people sell a herbal drink claiming it cures every illness; they call it a panacea.
Hope is related but not the meaning. A panacea is a cure.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in quotes: Jankoli was dressed in an old "assortment" of clothes.

options.why: Avalanche means a huge amount suddenly.
options.whyWrong: An avalanche is a sudden huge quantity, not a mixed collection.

options.why: Homogeneity means sameness, the opposite.
options.whyWrong: Homogeneity means all alike. An assortment is a mixture.

options.why: Sameness is the opposite.
options.whyWrong: Sameness is the opposite of an assortment.

options.why: A melange is a mixture of different things, like an assortment.

questions.explanation: An assortment is a mixed collection of different kinds of things. A melange is also a mixture.
questions.trap: B and C both mean sameness, which is the opposite. If two options mean the same thing, neither is likely the answer.

askPresets.answer: A pack of assorted biscuits has many different kinds mixed together.
Homogeneity means all alike. An assortment is a mixture.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option nearest in meaning to the word in quotes: The director's remark was extremely "apposite" to the issue being discussed.

options.why: Apposite means suitable and relevant, that is, appropriate.
Inconsequential means unimportant.
options.whyWrong: Inconsequential means not important, almost the opposite.

options.why: Emphatic means forceful.
options.whyWrong: Emphatic describes the way something is said, not how relevant it is.

options.why: Adequate means enough.
options.whyWrong: Adequate means just enough. Apposite means fitting and relevant.

questions.explanation: Apposite means highly suitable or relevant in the circumstances. Appropriate is the closest meaning.
questions.trap: Do not confuse apposite with opposite. They look alike but mean very different things.

askPresets.answer: A proverb that fits the situation exactly is apposite.
Adequate means just enough. Apposite means fitting and relevant.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the gap: He can recall the important dates in the nation's history; it is interesting to listen as he rattles ______.

options.why: To rattle off means to say a list quickly from memory.
Rattle over is not a correct phrasal verb.
options.whyWrong: "Rattle over" is not used in English. The phrasal verb is rattle off.

options.why: Rattle up is not correct here.
options.whyWrong: "Rattle up" does not mean listing from memory.

options.why: Rattle out is not the standard form.
options.whyWrong: The standard phrasal verb for reciting quickly is rattle off.

questions.explanation: To rattle something off means to say it quickly and easily from memory, like a list of dates.
questions.trap: D, out, sounds natural to many speakers, but the correct phrasal verb is rattle off.

askPresets.answer: Some students can rattle off the whole periodic table in one breath.
The standard phrasal verb for reciting quickly is rattle off.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the gap: A wide range of options ______ made available to students in the final year last year.

options.why: "Is" is singular but present tense.
options.whyWrong: The sentence says "last year", so we need the past tense. "Was" is correct.

options.why: "Were" agrees with options, but the subject is "range".
options.whyWrong: The subject is "a wide range", which is singular. "Of options" does not change the subject.

options.why: "Are" is plural and present.
options.whyWrong: Wrong number and wrong tense. Singular "range" and "last year" need "was".

options.why: The subject is the singular "a wide range", and "last year" needs the past tense.

questions.explanation: The subject of the sentence is "a wide range", which is singular; "of options" only describes it. "Last year" requires the past tense. So the verb is "was".
questions.trap: "Were" tempts students who make the verb agree with the nearest noun, "options". Find the real subject first.
questions.mnemonic: Ignore the "of" phrase to find the subject.

askPresets.answer: "A box of pens was stolen": the box was stolen, not "were".
The subject is "a wide range", which is singular. "Of options" does not change the subject.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The principal said that he was pleased ______ my effort.

options.why: "Pleased on" is not correct English.
options.whyWrong: "Pleased" is followed by "with", not "on".

options.why: "Pleased of" is not correct.
options.whyWrong: "Pleased of" is incorrect. We say pleased with.

options.why: "Pleased with" is the correct fixed preposition.
"Pleased at" is less standard here.
options.whyWrong: "Pleased at" is sometimes heard, but the standard form for someone's effort is pleased with.

questions.explanation: Some adjectives always take a particular preposition. We are pleased with someone or something.
questions.trap: "At" sounds acceptable in speech, but JAMB tests the standard form: pleased with.
questions.mnemonic: Pleased with, angry with, happy with.

askPresets.answer: Learn adjectives with their prepositions as pairs: pleased with, afraid of, interested in.
"Pleased at" is sometimes heard, but the standard form for someone's effort is pleased with.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the gap: They are the ______ dresses.

options.why: "Babys'" is not a correct spelling.
options.whyWrong: The plural of baby is babies, so "babys'" is never correct.

options.why: "Baby dresses" is possible, but the question tests the possessive.
options.whyWrong: "Baby dresses" uses baby as a describing word, but JAMB is testing the plural possessive form.

options.why: "Babies" is plural but not possessive.
options.whyWrong: Babies needs an apostrophe to show the dresses belong to them: babies'.

options.why: Plural possessive: the dresses belong to the babies.

questions.explanation: Plural of baby is babies. For a plural ending in -s, add only an apostrophe to show possession: babies'.
questions.trap: C, babies, has no apostrophe, so it does not show ownership.

askPresets.answer: One baby's dress; many babies' dresses.
Babies needs an apostrophe to show the dresses belong to them: babies'.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the gap: When we looked up, we ______ the plane some miles away.

options.why: A site is a place.
options.whyWrong: Site means a location, as in a building site. We need the verb that means saw.

options.why: Cited means quoted.
options.whyWrong: Cited means quoted as evidence, as in citing a book.

options.why: Sited means placed somewhere.
options.whyWrong: Sited means positioned, as in the school was sited near the river.

options.why: Sighted means saw or caught sight of.

questions.explanation: Site, cite and sight sound alike but mean different things. To sight something is to see it, so "we sighted the plane".
questions.trap: C, sited, sounds exactly the same as sighted. Homophone questions test spelling and meaning, not sound.
questions.mnemonic: Sight = see; site = place; cite = quote.

askPresets.answer: You sight a plane, visit a site and cite a source.
Sited means positioned, as in the school was sited near the river.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the gap: The federal government has ______ child trafficking.

options.why: Postulated means suggested as a theory.
options.whyWrong: To postulate is to propose an idea. Governments ban crimes, they do not postulate them.

options.why: Projected means forecast.
options.whyWrong: Projected means estimated for the future, which does not fit.

options.why: Prescribed means recommended or ordered.
options.whyWrong: Prescribed is the opposite: it means to order or recommend, like a doctor's prescription.

options.why: Proscribed means officially banned.

questions.explanation: Prescribe and proscribe look alike but are near opposites. To prescribe is to recommend; to proscribe is to forbid. The government has proscribed (banned) child trafficking.
questions.trap: C, prescribed, differs by one letter but means the opposite. Read each option slowly.

askPresets.answer: A doctor prescribes medicine; the law proscribes crime.
Prescribed is the opposite: it means to order or recommend, like a doctor's prescription.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that best completes the gap: Many people would always find reasons to ______ the law.

options.why: Arrogate means to claim without right.
options.whyWrong: To arrogate is to take power or rights you are not entitled to. It does not fit "the law".

options.why: Debase means to lower in value.
options.whyWrong: Debase means to lower the quality, which does not describe avoiding a law.

options.why: Circumvent means to find a way around a rule.
Circumspect is an adjective meaning careful.
options.whyWrong: Circumspect is an adjective, so it cannot follow "to" as a verb.

questions.explanation: To circumvent the law is to find a clever way around it, avoiding it without directly breaking it.
questions.trap: D, circumspect, looks similar but is an adjective meaning cautious. It cannot be used as a verb.

askPresets.answer: Using a back road to avoid a checkpoint is circumventing it.
Circumspect is an adjective, so it cannot follow "to" as a verb.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the underlined letters "ou" in: coup

options.why: Whup has the short vowel /ʌ/.
options.whyWrong: Whup has the vowel in "cup", not the long /uː/ of coup.

options.why: Coup is pronounced "koo", with long /uː/, the same as hoot.
Couple has /ʌ/, despite the same spelling.
options.whyWrong: Couple is spelt with "ou" but sounds like "cup". Spelling does not decide the sound.

options.why: Scout has the diphthong /aʊ/.
options.whyWrong: Scout rhymes with "out", a different sound from the long /uː/ in coup.

questions.explanation: Coup is a French word pronounced /kuː/ (the p is silent). Its vowel is the long /uː/ heard in hoot, food and moon.
questions.trap: C, couple, has the same spelling "ou" but a different sound. In oral English, never trust spelling.

askPresets.answer: The pigeon says "coo"; a coup sounds the same.
Couple is spelt with "ou" but sounds like "cup". Spelling does not decide the sound.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that has the same vowel sound as the underlined letter "i" in the second syllable of: indict

options.why: Indict is pronounced "in-DITE", with /aɪ/ as in bright.
Fish has the short /ɪ/.
options.whyWrong: Fish has the short "i" sound. The "i" in indict is pronounced like "eye".

options.why: Pick has the short /ɪ/.
options.whyWrong: Pick has the short "i". Indict has the diphthong /aɪ/.

options.why: Brick has the short /ɪ/.
options.whyWrong: Brick has the short "i", and its spelling with -ick fools students.

questions.explanation: Indict is pronounced /ɪnˈdaɪt/; the c is silent and the second syllable sounds like "dite". The vowel /aɪ/ is the same as in bright, kite and night.
questions.trap: D, brick, is tempting because indict is spelt with -ict. The c is silent and the vowel is /aɪ/.

askPresets.answer: Indict, invite, excite: same final sound.
Brick has the short "i", and its spelling with -ick fools students.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that has the same consonant sound as the underlined letter "h" in: high

options.why: In standard English the wh in what is /w/.
options.whyWrong: What starts with a /w/ sound in standard pronunciation, not /h/.

options.why: The h in honest is silent.
options.whyWrong: Honest starts with a vowel sound; the h is silent.

options.why: Who is pronounced "hoo", starting with /h/.
The h in vehicle is silent.
options.whyWrong: In vehicle the h is silent in standard pronunciation.

questions.explanation: High begins with the sound /h/. Who also begins with /h/ (the w is silent). Honest and vehicle have a silent h, and what begins with /w/.
questions.trap: B, honest, has the letter h but no /h/ sound. Silent letters are a favourite JAMB trap.
questions.mnemonic: Listen, don't look: who has /h/, honest does not.

askPresets.answer: Hour, honest and heir all have a silent h.
Honest starts with a vowel sound; the h is silent.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the option that rhymes with: shine

options.why: Clean has /iː/ and n, not the same vowel.
options.whyWrong: Clean ends in /iːn/, not /aɪn/.

options.why: Fine ends in /aɪn/, the same as shine.
Machine ends in /iːn/.
options.whyWrong: Machine is spelt with -ine but ends like "clean", /iːn/.

options.why: Lain ends in /eɪn/.
options.whyWrong: Lain ends in /eɪn/, like "rain".

questions.explanation: Words rhyme when their final vowel sound and following consonants match. Shine and fine both end in /aɪn/.
questions.trap: C, machine, is spelt with -ine like shine but is pronounced "ma-SHEEN".
questions.mnemonic: Rhyme by ear, not by eye.

askPresets.answer: Shine, fine, mine and line all rhyme.
Machine is spelt with -ine but ends like "clean", /iːn/.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the correct stress pattern. The stressed syllable is in capital letters: political

options.why: This stresses the third syllable.
options.whyWrong: Political is not stressed on "ti". The stress falls on "LI".

options.why: Political is stressed on the second syllable: po-LI-ti-cal.
This stresses the first syllable, as in the noun politics.
options.whyWrong: The noun POlitics is stressed on the first syllable, but adding -ical moves the stress: poLItical.

options.why: Stress on the last syllable is not used.
options.whyWrong: The ending -al is not stressed in English.

questions.explanation: Words ending in -ical are usually stressed on the syllable just before -ical: poLItical, ecoNOMical, hisTORical.
questions.trap: C copies the stress of POlitics. The suffix -ical shifts the stress forward.

askPresets.answer: poLItical, gramMAtical, hisTORical.
The noun POlitics is stressed on the first syllable, but adding -ical moves the stress: poLItical.

questions.subject: english
questions.stem: Choose the correct stress pattern. The stressed syllable is in capital letters: satisfactory

options.why: This stresses the second syllable.
options.whyWrong: SaTISfactory is incorrect. The main stress is on FAC.

options.why: Satisfactory is stressed on the third syllable: sa-tis-FAC-to-ry.
This copies the stress of SATisfy.
options.whyWrong: The verb SATisfy is stressed on the first syllable, but satisfactory moves it to FAC.
